summary: Defines an SMTP extension and header field, Require-Recipient-Valid-Since, that lets senders say when they knew who owned a mailbox. Receivers can detect changes of ownership and avoid delivering sensitive mail to the wrong person.

eli5.summary: Before handing over a private letter, you check that the mailbox still belongs to the same person as when you last wrote.

questions: how to prevent email going to new mailbox owner
how to stop email going to a reassigned address
subtitle: A way for a sender to say "I knew who owned this mailbox at this time", so mail is not delivered to a later owner.

tldr.problem: Email addresses get reassigned, so sensitive automatic mail such as password changes can reach the right address but the wrong person.
tldr.mechanism: The sender attaches a timestamp, either as an RRVS parameter on the SMTP RCPT command or in a Require-Recipient-Valid-Since header field. The receiver checks whether the mailbox has had one continuous owner since then and rejects the message if not.
tldr.outcome: Receivers can refuse delivery after an ownership change, but this is only a request to the receiver, and the timestamp itself can leak information about the mailbox.

facts.label: Auth-Results values
facts.value: none, unknown, temperror, permerror, pass, fail

today: RFC 7293 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2014, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself notes the privacy trade-offs, so it recommends using the header field only when the receiver is known to support it.

sections.title: The Problem of Reassigned Addresses
sections.content:
Email addresses sometimes get reassigned. An address used by an ex-employee may go to a new employee, or a mail service provider may expire an account and let someone else register the same local-part. Senders who wrote to the previous owner might not know. Mail then goes to the correct address but the wrong recipient, which is a particular worry for transactional mail about purchases and online accounts.

RFC 7293 lets the sender say, in effect, "I know the intended recipient was using this address at this point in time. I do not want this message delivered to anyone else." The receiving system compares that time with the time the address was assigned to its current user. If the assignment is later, it can block delivery and, preferably, tell the sender.

The primary use is automatically generated mail such as account information and password change requests, not user-written messages.
sections.eli5: Imagine your old neighbor moved out and a new family got the same mailbox. If you keep mailing secrets to that address, the new family reads them. This RFC lets you write on the envelope the date you knew your friend lived there.

sections.title: The RRVS Extension and the Header Field
sections.content:
Two mechanisms are defined. The RRVS SMTP extension is advertised with an extra EHLO keyword RRVS, which has no parameters, adds no commands and does not change the MAIL command. It adds one parameter to RCPT: a timestamp in the date-time format of RFC 3339, with no time-secfrac. The timestamp may be followed by a semicolon and a letter, the no-support action: R (reject, the default) or C (continue). The extension raises the maximum RCPT command length by 33 characters.

The Require-Recipient-Valid-Since header field carries an addr-spec and a timestamp in the message-header date format. It exists to tunnel the request through servers that do not support the extension. Because the field names the recipient address, it still works when the message is forwarded.

The extension gives strong assurance, since support is confirmed at each hop and the message can be returned if end-to-end support is missing. The header field is only best effort.
sections.eli5: There are two ways to write the date on the envelope. One is a note handed to the mail carrier at the door. The other is a note tucked inside the envelope, for carriers who do not know about the door note.

sections.title: What Continuous Ownership Means
sections.content:
An address has been under continuous ownership since a given time if a message sent to it at any point since then would not go to anyone except the owner at that time. The address may have been suspended for a while, as long as any mail actually delivered would have gone only to the same owner. How the receiver finds this out is a local matter outside the scope of the RFC.

The answer is "yes", "no" or "unknown", and what to do on "unknown" is local policy. Unknown can happen when a domain changes hands without mailbox history, or when the ownership database is temporarily unavailable, in which case normal SMTP temporary failure handling applies.

If an address has had one continuous owner since it was created, any confirmation time SHOULD pass, even one earlier than the account creation time. This avoids exposing account details.
sections.eli5: The question is simple: has this mailbox always belonged to the same person since the date on the note? The answer can be yes, no, or "we cannot tell".

sections.title: Handling the SMTP Extension
sections.content:
A receiving MTA or MDA that sees an RRVS parameter on RCPT TO checks whether the current owner has held the mailbox continuously back to the given time. An MDA first ignores the parameter if the mailbox is a role account listed in RFC 2142. Otherwise, if ownership has not been continuous, it returns a 550 error to the RCPT command.

An MTA that does not check ownership, such as one at an organizational boundary, SHOULD relay the parameter to the next hop. If the next hop does not advertise RRVS and the no-support action is absent or R, the MTA MUST reject, either with a 550 to the DATA command or by generating a Delivery Status Notification and stopping relay attempts. The no-support action MUST be preserved when relaying.

If the receiver never recorded when the mailbox was created or reassigned, the MDA picks the latest possible plausible time, such as the earliest recorded creation time. If no reasonable substitute exists, it rejects with a code saying the test cannot be completed. Generators and receivers MUST also keep clocks synchronized using a protocol such as NTP.
sections.eli5: The post office checks the date on the note against the date the mailbox changed hands. If the mailbox changed after the note's date, the letter is refused. Offices that cannot check pass the note along.

sections.title: Handling the Header Field
sections.content:
When no RRVS parameter was used, a receiver looks at the header fields. It extracts the fields for recipients without a matching SMTP parameter, then discards any that are syntactically invalid, name a role account, do not match a current RCPT TO recipient, or do not refer to a mailbox handled locally. For each remaining field it tests continuous ownership and rejects the message on failure.

It is RECOMMENDED to remove the field before delivery to a mailbox, or when forwarding to remove those fields that were not discarded. This is not mandatory because some agents cannot strip headers, and digital signatures might be invalidated. The field MUST NOT be covered by digital signatures.

The header field MUST NOT be used unless the originator or relay knows the receiving MDA or an intermediary MTA will apply it properly, and it SHOULD NOT be used for messages with multiple recipients. Doing so can expose one recipient's information to the others, and one failing recipient can cause delivery to fail for all recipients handled by the same server.
sections.eli5: If the note is inside the envelope, the mail room opens it, checks the date, and ideally throws the note away so nobody else reads it later.

sections.title: Relays, Aliases and Mailing Lists
sections.content:
An MTA holding an RRVS message that must be relayed to a server without RRVS support has three choices: decline to relay, preferably with a Delivery Status Notification (RECOMMENDED); downgrade to the header field (SHOULD NOT unless specific conditions hold); or silently continue, dropping the protection. Conversely, a server receiving the header field that relays to an RRVS-capable server SHOULD delete the field and use the extension. Doing so may break later header validation such as hashes.

Special addresses are covered too. Delivery to a mailing list counts as final delivery, and the participating MDA needs to omit the RRVS information when passing the message to the list service, since list output is a new message. For a single-recipient alias, the usual check is made, and if the relay confirms the new destination it SHOULD use the later of the two timestamps. Receivers SHOULD NOT introduce RRVS on messages that arrived without it.
sections.eli5: If the next post office does not understand the date note, the safest choice is to send the letter back. Passing it on anyway means giving up the protection.

sections.title: Examples and Authentication-Results
sections.content:
In the RFC's SMTP example the server advertises 250 RRVS, the client sends RCPT TO:<receiver@example.com> RRVS=2014-04-03T23:01:00Z, and the server answers 550 5.7.17 receiver@example.com is no longer valid. The header field example reaches the same rejection after DATA.

Results can be reported in an Authentication-Results header field with method rrvs. The result names are none, unknown, temperror, permerror, pass and fail. A pass does not reveal the timestamp.

IANA registered the extension, the header field, the method and result names, and three enhanced status codes: X.7.17 (mailbox owner has changed), X.7.18 (domain owner has changed) and X.7.19 (RRVS test cannot be completed).
sections.eli5: The post office answers with a short message such as "this mailbox is no longer valid", or with a stamp saying pass or fail.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Trade-offs
sections.content:
A server's response can disclose how old a mailbox is, so probing is a risk. Countermeasures are RECOMMENDED, for example ignoring the field and silently discarding the message if many timestamps are tried against one mailbox quickly. If a mailbox has had a single owner since creation, or did not exist before the timestamp, the field SHOULD be silently ignored so nothing is disclosed.

RRVS is only a request. A receiver may not implement it correctly, or may choose not to block delivery for local, legal or operational reasons, so senders may feel safer than they are. Senders do well to use it only with known, trusted receivers. A bad actor may also read its presence as a sign of high-value content, and the header field can reveal the intended recipients, or be forwarded by user agents that do not display it.

The RFC argues that exposing mailbox history is a far lower risk than delivering credentials to the wrong party. It also RECOMMENDS a substantial period between mailbox owners during which the mailbox accepts no mail.
sections.eli5: The date note could tell a nosy person how long a mailbox has been around, and it is only a request. Still, that is much less harmful than handing someone else your password letter.

data.title: RRVS syntax
data.code:
rrvs-param = "RRVS=" date-time [ ";" ( "C" / "R" ) ]

rrvs = "Require-Recipient-Valid-Since:" addr-spec ";" date-time
       CRLF

messages.label: 550 5.7.17 receiver@example.com is no longer valid
messages.note: Ownership was not continuous since the timestamp.
